analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the federal agency that studies toxic chemical exposure in communities.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, the federal agency that investigates how hazardous waste and toxic chemicals sicken people in nearby communities. A single representative introduced it on the first day of the 117th Congress. It moved no further than a referral to a subcommittee, with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been polluting industries and hazardous-waste handlers: the agency that documents chemical exposure sites and publishes health assessments about them would have been shut down, with only the narrow disease-exposure registries preserved elsewhere in the Department of Health and Human Services.

how_it_helps.text: It abolishes the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, effective one year after enactment, and terminates all of the agency's functions [S3].

It preserves only two narrow functions — the national registry of serious diseases and the national registry of persons exposed to toxic substances — by transferring them to another entity within the Department of Health and Human Services, and eliminates the agency's health assessment, consultation, and emergency-response work through a series of amendments to more than a dozen environmental and public health laws [S3].

The bill's conforming amendments strike the agency's role from laws covering hazardous waste, clean air, clean water, toxic substances, and public health, removing it from programs that assess chemical exposures in communities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on residents living near hazardous-waste sites, chemical releases, and toxic exposures, who would lose the independent federal agency that investigates whether their illnesses are linked to contamination, and on state and local health officials who rely on its assessments.

drawbacks.text: Abolishing the agency would have ended independent federal health assessments at hazardous-waste sites, leaving communities without the federal investigations that document links between toxic exposure and disease, since only the disease and exposure registries would have been transferred elsewhere [S3].

The registries would have been moved into the Department of Health and Human Services with no guarantee of dedicated staff, funding, or expertise, and the agency's site-specific public health work — including its assessments for communities near Superfund sites — would have simply terminated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have eliminated a small federal agency whose work exists to tell communities whether toxic contamination is making them sick, preserving only two registries. The savings would have been modest, and the loss — independent health investigation of chemical exposures — would have fallen on people with no other federal advocate. There is little argument in the record for the bill beyond its one-sentence goal of abolition; the House never gave it a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee on February 2, 2021, and stayed there until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 4, 2021, the first day of the 117th Congress, as his first bill of the session [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on February 2, 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it remained for the rest of the Congress [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, the bill's cosponsor list remained at zero, and no committee action, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The communities and the agency's mission lost nothing, because the bill went nowhere. Any polluting operations that would have benefited from the agency's absence were spared the need to do anything — no vote was ever held.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near toxic sites, since it died

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 4, 2021 to abolish the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry; it was his sole sponsorship and it attracted no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so party positions were never recorded; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of any party [S4].

industries.note: The agency the bill would abolish publishes health assessments and investigates chemical exposure at contaminated sites near communities, work that can trigger cleanup scrutiny and legal exposure for polluters. Shutting it down would have removed that independent federal examination of their operations.

industries.industry: Residents near Superfund and contaminated sites
industries.note: Not an industry, but the most affected group: the agency the bill would abolish is the federal body that investigates whether people near hazardous-waste sites are being poisoned, and it would have been gone.
